item.title: Class Attendance
item.description:
Most of the real work in this course happens in the room with your group. Attendance is taken each day while you work on your case analyses, and it counts toward your Class Engagement grade.

You get three (3) drops; no questions asked.

Attendance and exit tickets are linked: a ticket submitted on a day you weren’t in class earns no credit. If something comes up and you miss a meeting, contact Danny within 24 hours — that day’s exit ticket is typically excused unless missing class becomes a pattern.

item.title: Exit Tickets
item.description:
A short in-class response that closes each meeting: credit-based, low-stakes, one for every class day (42 across the semester). Credit means completion, not correctness, but you need to be in class to earn it; a ticket completed without attendance gets no credit for that day.

Exit tickets are completed on D2L and due by 5pm the day of class.

Exit tickets do double duty: they tell me what landed and what didn’t before the next class, and they give you a running record of your own thinking to draw on when you write your weekly forum post.

item.title: Forum Posts
item.description:
Each week there’s outside material to read, watch, or listen to. You respond to a posed question about that material in a roughly 250-word post, using evidence from the material and your own research, cited in APA format. This is also the main place you’ll do the metacognitive analysis described in the learning goals: how your own use of, and relationship to, these systems is shifting.

Forum posts are due on D2L before the first day of class each week (Sunday at 11:59pm).

item.title: Case Studies & Template
item.description: Most weeks begin with a particular AI‑in‑society use case presented by the instructor. In class, your group (3–4 students) analyzes the case using the DTPA framework, answering key questions with evidence. Early on, groups focus on one component of DTPA at a time (Data → Tools → Practices); later, groups apply the full framework and are expected to locate additional, related cases (e.g., voting, criminal‑justice, environment) to synthesize across uses.

item.title: Individual Effort & Metacognitive Report
item.description:
A short individual write-up (~250 words) that accompanies each week’s case study. Everyone in a group writes their own, and they are not shared with your groupmates.

Individual Effort & Metacognitive Reports are turned in on D2L as an individual upload, due 11:59pm the Sunday following that week’s classes.

Cover three things:

  • Effort — what did you actually contribute to the group’s case analysis?
  • Learning — how is your learning going on this week’s subject matter? What went well, what needs to improve?
  • Values — how do your own values and views shape the way you read this case?

You also need to disclose any AI use in your work here.

item.title: Lesson Planning & Leading Class
item.description:
After the first few weeks of class, groups of students (3–4) can opt in to plan and lead a lesson. Expect this to take each student roughly 10 hours to plan and lead. This is a deeper engagement option, not a requirement.

How to sign up

Reach out to your instructor at least two weeks before your planned lesson. A student may only participate once, and scheduling depends on availability, so your lesson may land later in the semester than you’d like.

item.title: Case Design & Template
item.description:
• Students: Teams of 3-4
  • Framework: Data-Tools-Practices-Actions (DTPA)

The Case Design project is the principal assessment for the course. Your team develops one case, in stages, over the whole semester. Your chosen topic must be substantial enough in scope to warrant a group effort.

Unlike Case Studies, this is not three separate documents. It is one document that grows: your Final Case Design is a direct expansion of your Scaffold 2, which is a direct expansion of your Scaffold 1. Each scaffold gets instructor feedback, and the next scaffold must respond to that feedback in a separate document.

item.title: Slides
item.description:
Slides

Every lecture deck is here in two forms.

  • Present opens the deck full-screen in your browser. Use the arrow keys or space bar to move between slides, f for fullscreen, and p for presenter view with speaker notes.
  • PDF downloads the same deck as a file. This is the version posted to D2L, so you do not need both.

Decks are posted after each class meeting. If a lecture is missing, it has not been given yet.

item.title: Week 1 Case Study: Data Collection and The Census
item.description:
All of this material is also available on Google Docs (MSU login required)

This Week’s Case

*Source: https://www.reddit.com/r/dataisbeautiful/comments/dbgg45/even_though_the_us_has_grown_in_every_census_some/

The U.S. Census of Population, 1790–today — and W.E.B. Du Bois’s data portraits of 1900.

Every ten years the federal government asks every person in the country to sort themselves into a set of boxes. Those boxes decide how $1.5 trillion in annual federal funding is distributed and how many seats in Congress each state gets. The boxes have changed almost every decade since 1790. Someone chooses them.

item.title: Week 2 Case Study: Neural Networks and Reading by Machine
item.description:
All of this material is also available on Google Docs (MSU login required)

This Week’s Case

Source: https://github.com/JoshEvan/Handwritten-Digits-Recognition-Using-Neural-Network-With-Tensorflow-and-Keras

Two systems that look at pixels and decide what they are: the U.S. Postal Service reading handwritten ZIP codes, and police departments running facial recognition.

These are close cousins. Both take an image, break it into a grid of numbers, and pass those numbers through layers of simple units until a label comes out the other end. The math is nearly the same. The neural network that reads your grandparents’s handwriting on an envelope is a direct ancestor of the one that scans a security camera still.

item.title: Resources
item.description:
📚 Curated Resources

Key Organizations & Research Centers

  • AI Now Institute — Research on AI’s societal impacts
  • Partnership on AI — Collaborative platform for responsible AI
  • Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET) — AI policy and safety
  • Stanford Internet Observatory — Tech policy research
  • Data & Society — Social implications of technology
  • Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) — Digital rights nonprofit; privacy, free expression, and surveillance litigation

Books

  • Weapons of Math Destruction — Cathy O’Neil, on how scoring algorithms in finance, policing, and education can quietly encode and amplify inequity
  • Automating Inequality — Virginia Eubanks, on algorithmic decision-making in the American welfare system
  • Race After Technology — Ruha Benjamin, on how bias gets built into tools that look neutral on the surface
  • Algorithms of Oppression — Safiya Umoja Noble, on how search engines reproduce racism and sexism
  • Atlas of AI — Kate Crawford, on the labor, data, and natural resources an AI system actually costs
  • Artificial Unintelligence: How Computers Misunderstand the World — Meredith Broussard, a data journalist’s case against “technochauvinism”
  • Artificial Intelligence: A Guide for Thinking Humans — Melanie Mitchell, the clearest plain-language account of how these systems actually work (and don’t)
  • The Age of Surveillance Capitalism — Shoshana Zuboff, on data extraction as a business model
  • The Ethics of Artificial Intelligence: Principles, Challenges, and Opportunities — Luciano Floridi (Oxford University Press), a short, structured overview of the ethical questions AI raises
  • The Internet Con: How to Seize the Means of Computation — Cory Doctorow, on monopoly power, platforms, and who actually controls the infrastructure AI runs on
  • The Reverse Centaur’s Guide to Life After AI - Cory Doctorow, on what happens next with AI and what we can do about it
  • Teaching Machines: The History of Personalized Learning — Audrey Watters, a history of ed-tech’s decades-old promises, well before Silicon Valley showed up

Podcasts

  • Your Undivided Attention — Center for Humane Technology; how technology is designed to capture attention, and what that design costs us
  • Tech Won’t Save Us — Paris Marx; a skeptical, historically grounded look at tech-industry narratives
  • This Machine Kills — Jathan Sadowski and Edward Ongweso Jr.; the political economy of technology
  • In Machines We Trust — MIT Technology Review, hosted by Jennifer Strong; AI’s everyday, on-the-ground impact
  • Better Offline — Ed Zitron; a critical read on the AI industry and its hype cycle
  • Kill Switch — iHeartPodcasts/Kaleidoscope, hosted by Dexter Thomas; a plain-language guide to the tech and algorithms running our lives
  • The 404 Media Podcast — the reporters behind 404 Media on the stories they’re breaking that week

News & Commentary

  • 404 Media — independent, journalist-owned outlet covering hacking, surveillance, AI, and platform power
  • MIT Technology Review — AI
  • The Verge — AI Coverage
  • Wired — AI

Tools & Platforms for Exploration

  • TensorFlow Playground — Interactive ML learning
  • Fast.ai — Free deep learning courses
  • Kaggle — Datasets and competitions

Additional resources will be shared throughout the course. Check D2L for week-specific readings and materials.

item.title: Syllabus
item.description:
Syllabus

AI in the Real World: Data, Power, & Society is a general education course that explores the conceptual foundations and societal implications of artificial intelligence. The course is designed to provide students with a critical understanding of how AI technologies are developed, deployed, and experienced in various social contexts. No programming experience is required, but students should be comfortable with basic computer literacy and have an interest in exploring the intersection of technology and society.

item.title: 1.1 Automated Essay Scoring (AES)
item.description:
Automated Essay Scoring (AES)

Context & Systems Architecture

Automated Essay Scoring (AES) systems utilize natural language processing (NLP) pipelines—ranging from traditional feature-extraction regression models (such as ETS’s e-rater) to fine-tuned transformer networks (such as BERT variants)—to evaluate student writing. These systems are widely deployed by major assessment corporations, including Pearson, ETS, and Turnitin, to grade high-volume standardized tests, admissions essays, and placement exams.

In a significant recent escalation of this technology, the Texas Education Agency deployed an automated scoring engine in 2024 to grade the State of Texas Assessments of Academic Readiness (STAAR) exams. The agency projected that the system would save $15–$20 million annually by reducing the number of human temporary graders from roughly 6,000 to under 2,000. However, the rollout resulted in widespread school district complaints after a dramatic surge in zero-scores for responses that did not fit the model’s expected syntax paths.

item.title: 1.2 AI Tutoring Systems
item.description:
AI Tutoring Systems

Context & Systems Architecture

AI tutoring systems have transitioned from rigid rule-based cognitive tutors to conversational platforms powered by large language models (LLMs). The most visible system is Khan Academy’s Khanmigo, introduced as a pilot in 2023. Khanmigo leverages foundational models (originally GPT-4, updated to GPT-4 Turbo and GPT-4o) bounded by system-level instructions that compel the AI to act as a Socratic guide rather than directly providing answers. The educational goal is to scale individual instruction to mitigate the post-pandemic learning loss.

item.title: 1.3 AI-Powered Exam Proctoring
item.description:
AI-Powered Exam Proctoring

Context & Systems Architecture

Remote exam proctoring applications (such as Proctorio, Honorlock, and Respondus Monitor) surged during the COVID-19 pandemic and continue to monitor high-stakes testing environments. These applications enforce academic integrity by locking down student web browsers and transforming the student’s personal webcam into a computer-vision surveillance apparatus. The software monitors eye movements, head orientation, ambient audio levels, and keyboard rhythms, automatically compiling a timeline of “suspicious events” for instructor review.

item.title: 1.4 Predictive Student Retention Systems
item.description:
Predictive Student Retention / Early Warning Systems

Context & Systems Architecture

Dozens of universities leverage enterprise predictive analytics platforms—such as EAB Navigate360 or Civitas Learning—to optimize student retention rates and allocate advising resources. By integrating directly with institutional Learning Management Systems (LMS) and student information databases, these platforms use historical enrollment logs to calculate a real-time “risk score” for every student, alerting advisors to individuals predicted to fail or drop out.

📘 Course Description

This course explores the complex interplay between artificial intelligence (AI) and modern society. Students examine AI’s applications, limitations, and implications across ethics, policy, economics, employment, and justice.

item.title: CMSE 101: Learning Goals
item.description:
Learning Goals

🦉 The Philosophy

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is not just a technical shift; it represents a fundamental restructuring of labor, power, and knowledge. Most MSU graduates will not be training AI models, but it is likely that they will be working alongside them. The suite of technologies that we call AI (e.g., machine learning, deep learning, generative AI) are not going back in the box, but we will eventually determine stable use cases for this tech.
